chapter_theme: The similes continue and then give way to the inner states themselves: the turtle whose thought hatches its eggs, butter that will not go back into buttermilk, light that swallows darkness, lightning in the sky, verdigris on copper, the mute's dream. From 187 the poet asks to leave even fixed meditation for the open space and the bare void, to see every form and every pleasure, even that of women, as the Lord, to know where sound and mind are born, to grasp awareness by awareness, and to see the dance that fills the worlds; the run ends with the comic heron glutted on fish.
structure_note: 176 to 185 open with a போல் simile; 186 to 199 are direct askings about states and places (the open space, the void, the hum and Om, the thousand-pillared hall); 200 returns to a simile. The refrain எக்காலம் closes every couplet.

176.reading: As the eggs with embryos take form when the sea turtle thinks of them, when will I reach you?
176.nuance: The turtle is said to hatch the eggs it laid on shore by thinking of them from the sea; the poet wants to be formed by the Lord's thought of him, or to reach him by his own thinking. The verse leaves it open who thinks.

177.reading: Like one who leaps out of the house and comes into the open, when will I know the sign for leaping out of the cage?
177.nuance: கூடு is the cage or nest, the body; the குறிப்பு is the sign or knack for leaving it. Tradition takes this as the yogic leaving of the body (the siddhi of entering another, or departing at will); plainly it is release from the body as such.

178.reading: As churned butter does not mix back into the buttermilk, when will I, broken free, see you, poor wretch that I am?
178.nuance: The butter image is of a separation that cannot be undone: once out, the soul does not return to the mixture. உடைந்து, broken, is the poet's own breaking out, or his being broken.

179.reading: As light swallows darkness and takes one form, when will the darkness that swallows grace depart and I stand?
179.nuance: The verb விழுங்கி is used twice, once for light eating darkness and once for the darkness that eats grace. The darkness that swallows grace is the primal mala in Siddhanta reading; the verse only calls it darkness.

180.reading: As lightning rises, lightning subsides and rests in the sky, when will I know within myself what stands within me?
180.nuance: The couplet is Sivavakkiyar's lightning verse compressed; the source marks it as a parallel. The Lord appears and withdraws within the poet as lightning does in the sky, which stays the same.

181.reading: As the sun's rays fall into water seen in a pot, when will I keenly know the form I have taken?
181.nuance: The one sun reflected in many pots is the Vedanta figure for the one self in many bodies. கொண்ட சொரூபம் may be the poet's own true form or the reflected one he has taken on; the verse asks to know which.

182.reading: When one wears the gold one puts on, does the gold carry the body? When will I see this in the thought that sees?
182.nuance: The rhetorical question seems to say that the body bears the ornament and not the reverse, so the body is the bearer and the ornament a weight; what the poet is to see in his thought is not stated, and the point may instead be that the gold is not changed by being worn.

183.reading: Like verdigris on copper, the three malas that have swallowed Siva and stand seething: when will I separate them off?
183.nuance: The three malas (anava, karma, maya) are named as மும்மலம். Verdigris is the metal's own corrosion, not a coating from outside, which fits the Siddhanta view that the malas are with the soul from the start.

184.reading: What stands in my soul as breath stands in the body: when will I, sinner, know it and hold my mind to it?
184.nuance: ஆவியும் காயமும்போல் gives the Lord's relation to the soul as the breath's to the body, inside and unseen; பாவி is the poet's name for himself.

185.reading: The joy that a mute who dreamed cannot tell: when will the day come for us to know it?
185.nuance: The mute's dream is a stock figure for an experience that cannot be reported; the poet asks for the experience, not the report.

186.reading: For those who never fail the feet of the undying Siva, when will it be that the body that does not go departs and goes?
186.nuance: போகா உடல் is the crux: a body that does not perish (the siddha's), or a body that will not let go. The line may ask when the devotee leaves the body for good, or when the imperishable body is itself left behind.

187.reading: Leaving fixed meditation, letting thought and knowing slip away, when will I stand mingled in the open space?
187.nuance: நிட்டை, the fixity of meditation, is itself to be left; the state asked for is past the practice, as in 151. வெட்டவெளி, the bare open space, is the Siddhars' name for the goal.

188.reading: The bare void that grew in the open space: when will I see it with resolve and become clear?
188.nuance: The void (பாழ்) is placed inside the open space (வெட்டவெளி) as something that arose there, and seeing it is to be done திட்டமுடன், deliberately; the void is a thing to be seen, not a lack.

189.reading: Everywhere as the supreme form, my form as your form, when will I see you without night or day?

190.reading: What I ate, and the pleasure I found joined with women: when will I see even these as you?
190.nuance: Food and sex are not renounced here but reread as the Lord; the verb is past tense (உண்டதுவும், கண்டதுவும்), so the pleasures may be past ones now to be understood, rather than a licence.

191.reading: What was heard as the hum, what stood within me, and what was said as Om: when will I reach and know them?
191.nuance: ஈம் is the inner hum (the nada heard in yoga), and ஓம் the uttered syllable; between them is what stands within. The verse asks whether the three are one thing.

192.reading: The place where sound was born, the place where it stood as its own nature, the place where the mind was born: when will I discern and know them?

193.reading: The one thing that strikes, standing as going and coming, as outside and inside: when will I meet it?
193.nuance: போக்கு வரவு is the out-and-in of the breath on a yogic reading, and the coming and going of births on a plain one. தாக்கும், strikes, suits the breath that beats in the body; the verse names neither.

194.reading: 'I' and 'you', 'we two', and the other one: when will it come right in my thought that all of these are you?
194.nuance: நாம் இரண்டு மற்றொன்றும், we two and a further one, makes three, which tradition matches to the Siddhanta triad; the verse resolves them into the one 'you', an advaitic move inside a work that elsewhere (153) keeps them apart.

195.reading: Knowing awareness by awareness, so that awareness does not stand parted within awareness: when will I hold it?
195.nuance: அறிவு occurs five times. The verse asks for knowing in which knower and known are not two, the state 158 approached from the side of forgetting speech.

196.reading: The holy dance that fills all the extended worlds and is red as vermilion: when will I know it?
196.nuance: சிந்தூரம் gives the dance a colour, red, the colour of the dancing Lord and of the dawn light in 171; the dance is cosmic here, not in the hall.

197.reading: The dance called thithi and the sounds of the holy anklets: when will I hear them with devotion and bow?
197.nuance: தித்தி is a dance syllable (the drum-sound to which the dance is set). The dance of 196 is now heard rather than known, and the response is bhakti.

198.reading: In the supreme space one reaches, like the space in the eye, when will I lie down and attain?
198.nuance: நயனத்திடை வெளி is the clear space within the eye, or the space between the eyes; tradition takes the second as the brow centre where the gaze is held. சயனித்து, lying down, is the yogi's rest in that space.

199.reading: In the thousand-pillared hall in the midst of the waterfall mountain, when will I see the holy play and have sight of it?
199.nuance: Plainly a shrine: a thousand-pillared hall on a hill with a waterfall, where the Lord's sports (திருவிளையாடல்) are seen. In cipher the thousand pillars are the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown and the waterfall the nectar that flows there. Both readings stand.

200.reading: Like a heron that ate too much fish and stands licking and hiccupping, when will I eat honey to surfeit and stand sated?
200.nuance: A comic self-portrait: the poet asks to be glutted on the honey of bliss as the heron is on fish. தெவிட்டி, cloyed, is a strong word for the fullness asked.

links.note: The sea turtle whose eggs on shore take form while it roams the sea, in both. Sivavakkiyar draws the lesson that thinking of the light within the body is the truth; Pattiragiriyar asks to be reached, or formed, in the same way.

Both use விழுங்கி, swallowing, for what the impurity does to the divine: the darkness swallows grace in 179, the three malas swallow Siva in 183. Together they give the lament's picture of the mala as an eater that must be cut away.

Pattiragiriyar's couplet is Sivavakkiyar's lightning verse in brief: lightning rises and subsides in the sky, and the Lord within subsides within. The source notes the parallel. Sivavakkiyar adds the eye that cannot see itself, which Pattiragiriyar omits.

Verdigris in both: Tirumular's Nandi cuts it away and opens the eye of grace; Pattiragiriyar names it as the three malas that have swallowed Siva and asks when he will separate them. In Tirumular the cutting is done by the guru, in Pattiragiriyar it is still asked for.

151 asks for what lies beyond eightfold yoga; 187 names the step, leaving fixed meditation (நிட்டை) and letting thought and knowing slip, to stand in the open space. The practice is left from inside it.

190 wants the pleasure found with women seen as the Lord; 211 wants the dream of desire for women removed. The conflict holds if 190 is read as a licence for present pleasure; if its past tenses mean pleasures already had and now to be understood, the two agree.

153 keeps the Siddhanta three apart, removing the bond and releasing the soul into the Lord; 194 resolves 'I', 'you' and the other into the one 'you'. They clash on the reading of 194 as an identity claim; if 194 only says the three are all his, 153's distinctions survive.

Both open with knowing awareness by awareness; 158 goes on to forgetting speech and sleeping, 195 to the condition that awareness not stand parted from awareness. The second states what the first's sleep contains.

Tirumular, having known himself, knew nothing else and was questioned through himself; Pattiragiriyar asks for awareness known by awareness with no parting within it. Both describe a knowing with no second thing in it.

Agasthiyar places the hum of Om at the centre of the brows and the fullness called Aum at the suzhumunai; Pattiragiriyar asks to know the hum he heard, what stood within and the Om he uttered as one. Both make the heard sound and the syllable the same thing in the body.

source_issues: 180 carries a PARALLELS note to siddhar:sivavakkiyam:124 (seq 1088); the couplet is a compression of that verse.
